items.bio: Studies fill placement and pacing to tune how an execution algorithm behaves.

journey.line: Dana Chen · Senior Execution Trader · Buy-side FX desk, London · EURUSD, 1M sell, one session
journey.scenario: Dana is working a 1M EURUSD sell across the London session. The algo slices it into child orders while she supervises a book of tickets at once. She starts from benchmarks she trusts, arrival mid and session TWAP, and steps in only when the canvas says the order needs her.
journey.goal: Finish inside the benchmarks, stay mostly passive, and defend the execution afterwards.
approachText: Post-trade learnings set the next order’s limit
quotes: “BARX fills me most. At what cost?”
“Act now, or wait one more bar?”

phases.title: Work the order
phases.description: Supervise one parent order from staging to done

steps.title: Pre-trade
steps.description: Dana reviews liquidity for the session and sets the order limit. Arrival mid anchors the execution; session TWAP provides an evolving market benchmark.
recommendations: Order ticket with limit and notional
Fixed arrival mid and evolving session TWAP
steps.backstage: The ticket carries the limit and notional. Arrival mid stays fixed; session TWAP updates as market prices arrive.

steps.title: Staging the order
steps.description: She stages the order straight from the chart, dragging the BID pill to a level and reviewing the pre-filled ticket before submitting.
recommendations: Pre-filled ticket, one check and go
steps.backstage: Dragging the BID pill stages the order at that level and pre-fills the ticket. Nothing is sent until she confirms.

steps.title: Working passively
steps.description: The algo works. Dana watches percent done against schedule, fills against the market, and the venue mix, without touching anything.
steps.backstage: The canvas draws percent done against schedule, fills sized by volume and coloured by venue, and the passive gauge updates as clips land.

steps.title: Intervention
steps.description: When the market drifts or a hatched band comes on, she acts from the chart: repricing the limit, flipping aggressive, or excluding a venue.
steps.backstage: Dragging the limit line opens a pre-filled reprice ticket. Confirmation and the audit trail stay on the chart.

steps.title: Post-trade review
steps.description: Done. Dana compares the order against its sibling, exports the fills, and writes the best-ex note while the context is fresh.
steps.backstage: Compare orders puts the sibling beside it with the benchmark metrics in one table. The table view exports the fills as CSV.

decisions.title: Progress and price on one canvas, not two panels

choices.label: One canvas with a dual axis
choices.alt: One canvas with price lines, a stepped limit and order progress on a dual axis.

choices.label: Two linked panels
choices.alt: Two linked panels separate market prices from execution progress.

decisions.reason: I explored two linked panels and one combined chart. I chose the combined canvas to keep price and progress in the same field of view. The trade-off was a denser chart that needed careful hierarchy.
decisions.tradeoff: A denser screen that needed careful hierarchy.
decisions.outcome: One canvas with a dual axis went in as the build contract. Readable in two seconds, actionable in one click.

decisions.title: Reprice on the chart, not in a settings menu

choices.label: Drag-to-reprice on the price line
choices.alt: Dragging the limit line opens a pre-filled reprice ticket beside the chart.

choices.label: A menu-based edit
choices.alt: A separate order-settings menu edits the limit price away from the chart.

decisions.reason: The limit price log showed orders being changed mid-flight. I reviewed a menu-based edit and drag-to-reprice with the business and charting vendor. I chose drag so the action stayed beside the price the trader was watching.
decisions.tradeoff: Drag needs a safety step, so a pre-filled ticket sits between the gesture and the change.
decisions.outcome: Drag-to-reprice went into the spec as the build contract. Each step commits you a little more, so you can’t reprice by accident.

decisions.title: Studies on market prices only. A decision I reversed

choices.label: Bid, ask and mid only
choices.alt: The study-source picker offers bid, ask and mid market prices.

choices.label: Any series, including the order’s own fills
choices.alt: The alternative allows own fills, whose data gaps make the study unreliable.

decisions.reason: My spec let analytics studies run on any series, including the order’s own fills. The vendor showed that order data has gaps, so a study on it looks confident and is wrong. I reversed it.
decisions.tradeoff: Less flexibility. Studies cannot run on the order’s own fills, even when someone asks for it.
decisions.outcome: I changed the specification to use bid, ask and mid as study inputs. The current public rebuild does not include the study-source picker.

decisionFlowText: Working Order Live → Watch the canvas. Percent done against schedule, fills against the market.
Percent done on schedule? On schedule → watch the canvas. Behind → is the average fill inside the benchmarks, arrival and TWAP?
Acceptable → stay passive: let resting limits work, keep working, watch the canvas.

Adverse → how to intervene? Reprice by dragging the limit line. Stage an order by dragging the BID pill. Fill now and take liquidity. Cross-filter venues to exclude poor fills. Each leads to Filled, Post-trade review.
Hatched band on: delayed, suspended, or outside limit → reprice, or accept the wait → keep watching. Session ends → cut off, fill now, or carry the risk.

items.bio: Uses the client-facing view in phase two, without the training available to internal analysts.

journey.line: Helen Marsh · Portfolio Manager · Asset manager, London · Quarterly board pack, one afternoon
journey.scenario: Helen is preparing a quarterly board meeting. She opens Fusion to pull performance, attribution and risk for the book, slices by asset class and period, and builds the view she will present live while the numbers are still updating.
journey.goal: Walk into the board meeting with numbers she trusts, built in one surface, without a spreadsheet detour.
approachText: Refine the view, back to filters
Phase two reuses the same screens

phases.title: Build the view
phases.description: Cube, filters and widgets in one surface

steps.title: Find the data
steps.description: Helen selects the data cube for her book. FactSet's engine feeds it, so the shape of the data is fixed and the first useful view has to be fast.
steps.backstage: FactSet engine returns the cube. The shape of the data is fixed, so the first view has to be fast.

steps.title: Shape the view
steps.description: Filter and slice: asset class, period, benchmark. The old RaaS layout couldn't flex to different data or roles.
recommendations: Comparison tools tailored to data complexity and role
steps.backstage: Salt filter bar and toggles. Entitlements decide which options each person sees.

steps.title: Analyse
steps.description: Returns, attribution and risk across asset classes, in widgets that work across cubes and permission levels.
recommendations: Data tables and chart frames on Salt
steps.backstage: One widget shell renders a table or a chart from the same data contract, across cubes.

steps.title: Present
steps.description: She presents the screen live, under pressure. Type, hierarchy and colour were set for this moment, not the clean demo.
recommendations: Board-ready report without leaving the surface
Worst-case viewing moment as the baseline
steps.backstage: Dashboard page configuration saved per user. Accessibility specialist reviews before release.

steps.title: Share and reuse
steps.description: Phase two: the same screens reach external clients who had no training. One codebase, entitlement decides what each person sees.
recommendations: Same patterns for internal and external users
Patterns reused across other Fusion modules
steps.backstage: One codebase. Entitlement-based views for clients. Import and export through FactSet.

takeaways.label: Opportunities
takeaways.text: Get in front of end users directly and earlier. The start leaned on product-owner requirements. Ship a leaner version one with fewer modules, and keep the accessibility specialist involved from the first review.

decisions.title: Dashboard structure

choices.label: Fixed layouts per report type
transcript: Fixed layout. New data cube = new page.

decisions.reason: We explored fixed layouts per report type and a widget grid. Fixed layouts were faster to ship, but every new data cube would have needed a new page. The grid won because one widget serves many cubes and permission levels.
decisions.tradeoff: Slower to ship than fixed layouts, and every widget had to earn its place in one of the four workflow steps.
decisions.outcome: Widget and filtering patterns reused across other Fusion modules.

decisions.title: Configuration
decisions.reason: Early versions had three levels of configuration. Testing showed the middle tier added cognitive load without changing what people built. I removed it. The test I use for what not to design: is this serving a real workflow contradiction, or one team's preference?
decisions.tradeoff: Fewer options for power users who liked the middle tier.
decisions.outcome: The first useful view was faster to reach.

decisions.title: Phase two
decisions.reason: Phase two brought in clients who'd had no training. We chose one product with entitlement-based views over a simplified client version, so patterns stayed consistent and the team kept one codebase.
decisions.tradeoff: Client constraints live in the same codebase as the internal views.
decisions.outcome: Phase two opened the product to external clients.

personas.intro: My two design personas: a designer like me and the developer who inspects the output. Role-based working assumptions the private alpha exists to test, not research participants.

items.name: Mei Lin
items.role:
Product Designer
Works inside a design system

groups.label: Goals
items: Prompt, generate, compare, tune, export
See the same screen in Salt, Material, Fluent and Carbon
Stay in control without making the AI useless

groups.label: Frictions

Designing for yourself hides your blind spots
Free-form generated UI looked impressive and was unusable

groups.label: In this app
items: A compare step across systems
Tune density, theme and charts
Mapped system components, with explicit fallbacks

items.bio: Designs screens inside an established design system, comparing and refining generated drafts.

items.name: Dev Patel
items.quote: “Show me code I recognise, not a picture of a screen.”

groups.label: Goals
items: Inspect the exported React
Recognise mapped components and inspect the fallbacks
Close the gap between a Figma file and code

groups.label: Frictions
items: Generated screens that use none of the team's components
Screens nobody tested with a user
A Figma file with nothing to inspect

groups.label: In this app
items: Export React a developer recognises
Native component mappings and explicit export fallbacks
Token mapping underneath, mapped not generated

items.bio: Receives exported React and needs to understand the components, structure and remaining work.

journey.line: Mei Lin · Product Designer · Works inside a design system · One screen in Salt, a Material version due, one afternoon
journey.scenario: Mei has a screen to design in Salt by Friday and a Material version due for a sister team. She describes the screen, reviews the generated canvas, compares the systems, tunes density and theme, and chooses when to export React for a developer to inspect.
journey.goal: Reach a useful, inspectable screen in a real design system without rebuilding it by hand for every system.
approachText: Alpha feedback changes the compare step
quotes: “That is a draft, not an answer.”
“I would never ship the first answer.”
“Does it work without me guiding it?”

phases.title: Draft
phases.description: Prompt and generate a structured canvas

steps.title: Prompt
steps.description: Mei describes the screen in words. The output can't be fully predicted, so the prompt has to say what matters: system, density, data.
recommendations: Name the system and density in the prompt
steps.backstage: The prompt is read with the system, density and data named, so the draft starts inside the right constraints.

steps.title: Generate
steps.description: The model adds structured blocks to the canvas. Supported combinations render real system components; other combinations use explicit fallbacks.
recommendations: Map supported blocks to native components
The first answer is a draft
steps.backstage: Claude uses the builder’s block catalogue and canvas tools. Component mappings and fallback renderers turn that structure into the screen.

steps.title: Compare systems
steps.description: The same screen in Salt, Material, Fluent and Carbon. The hard part is where the systems disagree.
steps.backstage: The same canvas maps to five systems. Each mapping uses the system’s component and layout APIs where available, with CSS or generic output for unsupported combinations.

steps.title: Tune
steps.description: Density, theme and charts. This is where the person decides, and where Mei corrects the model most often.
recommendations: Compare and tune before choosing to export
steps.backstage: Density, theme and chart props re-render the same component tree. Nothing is redrawn by hand.

steps.title: Export React
steps.description: Code a developer recognises. It closes the gap between a Figma file and the thing a developer can inspect.
steps.backstage: React export includes component mappings and styles, with fallbacks where needed. Export is available directly; the product does not enforce a compare-and-tune gate.

takeaways.label: Opportunities
takeaways.text: The next validation question: can another designer reach a useful, inspectable screen without me guiding them? The private alpha exists to answer it, and to break my own assumptions.

decisions.title: Generation

choices.label: Mapped components with explicit fallbacks
transcript: Supported blocks map to native components; uncovered combinations use fallbacks

choices.label: Letting the model draw free-form UI
transcript: A visual draft without recognised component mappings

decisions.reason: I chose a structured block model rather than arbitrary generated UI. Supported blocks map to native system components. The renderer and exporter use explicit fallbacks where a system has no equivalent.
decisions.tradeoff: Mappings need maintenance, and fallback output still needs inspection before handover.
decisions.outcome: The output is something a developer recognises and can inspect.

decisions.title: Switching systems

choices.label: Five systems, one model underneath
transcript: Switch system, density or theme without a hand rebuild

decisions.reason: I mapped the same canvas to the supported systems, each with its own components, density and theme rules. Switching systems preserves the structure so the designer can inspect the differences.
decisions.tradeoff: The systems do not map one to one. Unsupported combinations need a fallback and a design decision.
decisions.outcome: Switch system, density or theme and the screen rebuilds without a hand rebuild.

decisions.title: Export

choices.label: Compare and tune before export
transcript: The person decides where the systems disagree

choices.label: The model's first answer
transcript: A first draft can be exported directly; review remains the designer’s responsibility

decisions.reason: I treat the first answer as a draft. Comparing systems and tuning the screen helps me review it before handover. The product leaves export available, so the person chooses when to use it.
decisions.tradeoff: Review takes time, and keeping export available means the person can also export without reviewing.
decisions.outcome: The compare and tune steps are where the person decides, and where I correct the model most often.

decisionFlowText: Map supported blocks to native components
Export is available directly; review is not an enforced gate

Never opted in

groups.label: Wants

Same screen, same stars
From their own phone

items.bio: Joins an existing family board as a partner, grandparent or childminder.

journey.line: An iPhone family scenario: set up once, repeat each day, and share the same board.
journey.scenario: A parent can explore the optional Sample Family or create a family directly. This scenario follows their own board into the daily routine and weekly progress. A second adult can join once the board exists.
journey.goal: Help a child recognise and complete routines, make progress visible, and let another adult pick up on the same board.
approachText: Stars contribute to weekly pet growth; a new egg arrives on Monday
A second adult joins the existing family board

phases.title: First week
phases.description: From a bad bedtime to the first reveal

phases.title: Keep coming back
phases.description: The weekly loop and the second adult

steps.title: Another bad bedtime
steps.description: Looks for a routine board after another difficult bedtime. The charts this family has tried have not held the child’s attention.
recommendations: Ad-free, kid-first on the store page
steps.backstage: App Store listing in the Kids Category: ad-free, no tracking, privacy manifest.

steps.title: First open
steps.description: Chooses Try the Sample Family on the welcome screen to inspect the routines and pet, then starts their own family setup.
recommendations: Add your own family when you like it
steps.backstage: The optional demo route loads a predefined Sample Family. Create Family is a separate route; the demo is not automatically seeded into a new board.

steps.title: First tick
steps.description: Hands the phone over. The child taps teeth. A star lands and confetti fires. Child feels delighted.
steps.backstage: The tick writes to the shared board. Confetti stays off when Calm Mode or Reduce Motion is enabled.

steps.title: End of day
steps.description: Checks Home for the week’s progress. In this scenario enough stars have been earned for the pet to grow, and enough completed routines for a treasure.
recommendations: No star penalty for a missed day
The pet grows on what was done
steps.backstage: The pet grows at star thresholds; treasures unlock from cumulative completed routines. The day rolls over at local midnight.

steps.title: End of week
steps.description: Prints the weekly summary for the fridge. Monday, a new pet arrives. Child feels excited.
recommendations: Old pet joins the Pet Pals collection
steps.backstage: Weekly summary printed. A new egg on Monday; the old pet joins Pet Pals.

steps.title: Second adult joins
steps.description: Invites grandma to the board. She opens it and ticks a bath. Child feels relieved, and a bit smug.
steps.backstage: Invite link joins the same board. Offline ticks queue and sync on reconnect through Firebase.

takeaways.label: Opportunities
takeaways.text: I want to check the pet helper text at small sizes and review the translated pet names with native speakers. The source now includes translations, but that does not establish that every label reads well.

decisions.title: Daily motivation

choices.label: Stars and a pet
transcript: Tap a routine, a star lands
What I saw in my own family
I explored icons, stickers and celebration to make a completed routine visible.
Each tap is a small win the child can see
Stars count towards the weekly pet, so the board has a reason to fill up.

choices.label: A plain tick list
transcript: A plain list marks completion. I wanted a more visible reward after the tap.

decisions.reason: Explored a plain tick list. Research on five to seven year olds said big icons, stickers and celebration win. The checklist lost in our own house within a week.
decisions.tradeoff: More art, motion and growth states to build and keep consistent than a plain checklist.
decisions.outcome: Routines ticked without nagging in our own house.

decisions.title: First open

choices.label: Optional Sample Family before personal setup
transcript: The welcome screen offers a Sample Family to try, or a direct route to create your own family.
A week of routines and stars

choices.label: A tour and an empty state
transcript: Routines live here. Tap to add one when you are ready.
A tour and an empty state
Both ask parents to invest before they have seen the loop. An empty board says nothing about why a child would care.
Add a child before anything shows
No pet, no stars, no week to look at

decisions.reason: I offer the Sample Family before personal setup so a parent can inspect the loop. Trying it is optional: the welcome screen also lets them create their family directly.
decisions.tradeoff: The example and the family’s own board are separate. The transition needs to make clear which actions will save real progress.
decisions.outcome: The welcome screen offers both a sample experience and direct family creation.

decisions.title: Access and trust

choices.label: Lifetime unlock
transcript: Free to start, one payment if you want everything. No ads, no third-party tracking.
Their kids are not the product

choices.label: A small subscription
transcript: Recurring payment adds another subscription for a parent to manage. I chose a one-off unlock.
A trial that turns into a charge

decisions.reason: It's for children, and trust is the product. Free to start, one payment if you want everything, no ads, no third-party tracking.
decisions.tradeoff: No recurring revenue.
decisions.outcome: Free to start, one payment if you want everything, no ads, no third-party tracking.

decisions.title: A theme per child

choices.label: A theme per child, drawn not templated
transcript: Illustrated themes include Football, Dinosaur, Ocean, Unicorn and Robot, with a photo avatar option.
Colour and picture beside the name

choices.label: One look for all
transcript: One treatment is simpler to maintain. It gives children fewer visual cues beside their name.
Fewer cues to recognise a card

decisions.reason: Explored one look for all. Kids find their own card by colour and picture before they can read. Fourteen illustrated banners, from Football and Dinosaur to Ocean, Unicorn and Robot, plus a photo avatar if they want their own face on it.
decisions.tradeoff: Fourteen illustrated banners to draw and keep consistent.
decisions.outcome: Kids find their own card by colour and picture before they can read.

decisions.title: A parental gate

choices.label: A quick maths question gates the exits
transcript: A speed bump, not a lock
A quick question adds friction to protected actions. It is not age verification or a security guarantee.

choices.label: A PIN, or a locked app
transcript: A PIN, or a locked app
A PIN adds a code to remember and a recovery flow. I wanted a quicker route for the adult.

decisions.reason: Explored a PIN. Parents forget PINs and kids watch them type. A quick maths question gates anything that leaves the app, uploads a photo or deletes an account, and Kid Mode locks editing so the phone can be handed over mid-routine.
decisions.tradeoff: A maths question is a speed bump for parents too.
decisions.outcome: Kid Mode lets the phone be handed over mid-routine.

decisions.title: Weekly pet

choices.label: A weekly pet with four stages
transcript: Stars count up and never down. One missed bath does not end the week, and Monday always brings a new egg.
A daily number resets at midnight. A pet that grows across the week survives a bad Tuesday.

choices.label: A daily score
transcript: Missed bath and reading. Score reset.
A daily score resets at midnight. I wanted completed routines to contribute across the week.

decisions.reason: I wanted the pet to grow from completed routines across the week. Missing a routine does not deduct stars, although a completed tick can be undone. Monday starts a new weekly pet.
decisions.tradeoff: No daily pressure means less urgency on a quiet day.
decisions.outcome: One missed bath does not end the week, and Monday always brings a new egg.

decisionFlowText: Optional Sample Family, or create your own family

items.bio: Owns the portfolio and platform, balancing the needs of sales, operations and legal.

journey.line: The deal owner · Custody sales · London · Global custody deal, four teams, one platform
journey.scenario: A client asks for a reprice before a call. The deal owner opens the deal, loads the portfolio, builds a new iteration on the benchmark rate card, compares it with the last two, and sends it for approval.
journey.goal: Price the deal, explain the selected iteration, and get a recorded approval with the comparison and comments in view.
approachText: Fix at the field, back to pricing
Upload template brings the last across
quotes: “Will product recognise this as a deal?”
“Do I have to key all this in again?”
“Three versions, so I can say what is wrong.”
“Audit can have this as it is.”

phases.title: Build the deal
phases.description: Create, load and price in one object

steps.title: Create the deal
steps.description: The deal owner creates the deal: name, region, segment, lead. Before, every team set a deal up its own way.
recommendations: Status and deal lead on the landing page
steps.backstage: Deal object created with role-based views. Deal team and status stored once.

steps.title: Load the portfolio
steps.description: Loads holdings and transactions, or uploads the filled template the system maps. Before, hand-keyed from a spreadsheet.
recommendations: Upload template, mapped by the system
steps.backstage: Mapping translates the uploaded template into the deal data model.

steps.title: Price and iterate
steps.description: Builds iterations from rate cards. The original design warns when the transaction rate differs from the SK rate, so the owner can review that difference.
steps.backstage: Iteration creation reports success or failure. The pricing design includes a warning when TXN rate differs from SK rate.

steps.title: Compare and tier
steps.description: Puts iterations side by side in the compare grid, chooses columns, applies tiering across AUC and transactions.
recommendations: Compare grid with a column chooser
steps.backstage: Grid settings saved per user. Tiering rules by AUC band and transaction type.

steps.title: Approve and sign off
steps.description: Writes a short winning-bid reason and publishes the selected iteration. The approver reviews the comparison and comments, then records a decision.
recommendations: Comparison and comments visible during review
Owner-written reason kept with the iteration
steps.backstage: The published iteration carries the owner’s reason. The approver reviews the comparison and comments; the product records the approval decision.

takeaways.label: Opportunities
takeaways.text: Keep pricing warnings close to the work. Make comparison a view, not a rebuild. Keep the owner’s reason with the iteration the approver reviews.

decisions.title: One object, four views

choices.label: One deal object with role-based views
transcript: One object underneath. The view changes, the deal does not.

decisions.reason: We explored one product per team and one deal object with four views. Most of the arguments were about columns, not about the deal. Once each team saw its own view of the same object, the fight went away.
decisions.tradeoff: Every change to the object needs all four teams in the review, so reviews are slower.
decisions.outcome: The four teams work on the same deal, and the audit trail is one trail.

decisions.title: Three versions, every review

choices.label: Three versions on the table
transcript: Ops: "B, but keep the totals row from A." Legal: "C hides the history."

choices.label: One proposal, sign-off at the end

decisions.reason: I ran every review with three versions. People said what was wrong instead of saying yes. Sales got the comparison table, legal got the iteration list, because they asked for them in those rooms.
decisions.tradeoff: Three versions is three times the preparation, every review, for a year.
decisions.outcome: The reviews shaped the comparison table and iteration list. I did not measure how much rework the method saved.

decisions.title: A compare grid with a column chooser

choices.label: Configurable compare grid
transcript: Saved per user. Sales keeps the comparison it needs.

decisions.reason: Sales rebuilt the comparison in Excel every time because the report never had the right columns. A grid with a column chooser, saved per user, made the comparison a view instead of a rebuild.
decisions.tradeoff: Saved settings per user and more states to design: empty, too many columns, a column that no longer exists.
decisions.outcome: The comparison became a configurable view of the iterations. I did not measure a separate impact for this feature.

decisions.title: An upload template, not a forced migration

choices.label: Upload the template, system maps it
transcript: Meet people where they are, then bring them over.

choices.label: Cut everyone over on day one

decisions.reason: Some people kept the spreadsheet. We built an upload template they could fill in, and the system mapped it to the data model. Meet people where they are, then bring them over.
decisions.tradeoff: Two ways in, so the mapping rules had to be maintained alongside the product.
decisions.outcome: The last people came across. If asked about adoption, the template is the answer.

decisions.title: Pricing feedback and an owner-written reason

choices.label: Owner: publish the proposal with a reason
transcript: Review the financial summary and approval level
choices.alt: Original Deal Model owner screen selecting an iteration and publishing the proposal for approval.

choices.label: Approver: review the proposal and comments
choices.alt: Original Deal Model approver dialog showing comments, a quick overview, the proposed bid and the owner-written winning-bid reason.

decisions.reason: I kept pricing feedback close to the work and the owner’s explanation with the selected iteration. The original flow has the owner write the winning-bid reason and publish it; the approver sees the comparison and comments before deciding.
decisions.tradeoff: The owner still has to explain the choice. Pricing warnings, creation errors and approval need distinct states so one is not mistaken for another.
decisions.outcome: The original design keeps the owner’s reason and iteration comparison available to the approver. It does not automatically write the sign-off narrative.

decisions.title: Smart pricing, explored

choices.label: Smart-pricing exploration
choices.alt: Original SmartPricing Reductions concept: a New Iteration dialog with reduction inputs, target fee type, markets and pricing influence.

choices.label: New-proposal exploration
choices.alt: Original SmartPricing New Proposal concept: portfolio selection, model scope, a price-all-markets checkbox and five iteration levels.

decisions.reason: At the end we explored training a model on past deals to suggest an iteration, with the deal owner editing or discarding it. Designed with the data analyst and reviewed with the four teams.
decisions.tradeoff: It needs clean historical data, which we were still assembling. The suggestion must never auto-apply.
decisions.outcome: Designed and reviewed, not built in my time. The same pattern I use in uoaui.ai: the model drafts, I decide.
